lessons.title: Landforms and Plate Tectonics
lessons.diagram: PLATE BOUNDARIES\\n\\n   CONVERGENT (collide → mountains)\\n   ┌────┐┌────┐\\n   │    ││    │  → ╱╲ mountains\\n   │ →  ││  ← │    ╱╲\\n   └────┘└────┘\\n\\n   DIVERGENT (pull apart → rift)\\n   ┌────┐  ┌────┐\\n   │  ← │  │ →  │  → rift valley\\n   └────┘  └────┘\\n\\n   TRANSFORM (slide past)\\n   ┌────┐\\n   │  → │───→\\n   └────┘\\n   ←───┌────┐\\n       │ ←  │\\n       └────┘
lessons.content: Earth's surface shaped by tectonic plates. Colliding plates → mountains (Himalayas). Pulling apart → rift valleys (East African Rift). Subduction → volcanoes and trenches. Earthquakes at boundaries. Weathering breaks rock, erosion transports material. Over millions of years, these forces create the landscapes we see today.
examples: Himalayas grow ~1cm/year from plate collision
East African Rift splitting the continent
Grand Canyon: 5-6 million years of erosion

keyTerms.tectonic plates: Large crust pieces moving slowly on the mantle
keyTerms.erosion: Wearing away and transport of rock/soil by water, wind, ice
keyTerms.volcano: Opening where magma reaches the surface, often at plate boundaries
keyTerms.weathering: Breaking down of rocks by physical, chemical, or biological processes

quiz.question: Mountains form when plates:
quiz.explanation: Crust crumples upward.

quiz.question: East African Rift:
quiz.explanation: Divergent boundary.

quiz.question: Erosion caused by:
quiz.explanation: These agents wear away and transport material.

quiz.question: The Ring of Fire is:
options: A zone of volcanic and earthquake activity around the Pacific Ocean
quiz.explanation: About 75% of the world's volcanoes and 90% of earthquakes occur along the Pacific Ring of Fire.

quiz.question: Weathering differs from erosion because:
options: Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion transports the pieces
Erosion breaks rock; weathering transports it
quiz.explanation: Weathering = breaking down. Erosion = carrying away. Different processes.

lessons.title: Weather and Climate
lessons.diagram: THE WATER CYCLE\\n\\n   ☀ Sun heats water\\n         │\\n    ╭────┴────╮\\n    │CONDENSATION│ ← clouds form\\n    ╰────┬────╯\\n         │\\n    ┌────▼────┐\\n    │PRECIPIT-│ ← rain/snow\\n    │  ATION  │\\n    └────┬────┘\\n         │\\n   ~~~COLLECTION~~~ ← rivers,\\n         │            lakes,\\n    ┌────▼────┐        oceans\\n    │EVAPORAT-│\\n    │  ION    │ ← water → vapour\\n    └─────────┘
lessons.content: Weather is day-to-day atmosphere (temperature, rain, wind). Climate is 30+ year average. Factors: latitude (equator = hotter), altitude (higher = cooler), distance from sea (coastal = milder), ocean currents, prevailing winds. Climate zones: tropical, arid, temperate, polar. Water cycle: evaporation → condensation → precipitation → collection → repeat.
examples: Kampala (equator): tropical, warm year-round
Kilimanjaro: snow despite being near equator — altitude
London: temperate maritime — mild, rainy

keyTerms.climate zone: Region with similar long-term weather patterns
keyTerms.prevailing wind: The most common wind direction in an area

quiz.question: Weather vs climate:
options: Weather is daily; climate is long-term average
quiz.explanation: Weather = today, climate = decades.

quiz.question: Higher altitude means:
quiz.explanation: ~6.5°C drop per 1000m.

quiz.question: Water cycle driven by:
quiz.explanation: Sun's heat causes evaporation.

quiz.question: Coastal areas have milder climates because:
options: Water heats and cools slowly, moderating nearby temperatures
quiz.explanation: Oceanic influence reduces temperature extremes.

quiz.question: El Niño affects weather by:
options: Changing Pacific Ocean temperatures, disrupting global weather patterns
quiz.explanation: El Niño warms Pacific waters, changing rainfall and temperature worldwide.

lessons.title: Rivers and Water Systems
lessons.content: Rivers have three stages: upper (steep, V-shaped, waterfalls), middle (wider, meanders), lower (flat floodplain, delta). Rivers erode, transport, deposit. Flooding from heavy rain or snowmelt. Floodplains are fertile from silt deposits. Drainage basins collect all water into one river. Rivers provide drinking water, irrigation, transport, hydroelectric power.
examples: Nile: 6,650 km, 11 countries
Meanders: outer bank erodes, inner bank deposits
Amazon discharges more water than next 7 rivers combined

keyTerms.meander: River curve from erosion and deposition
keyTerms.floodplain: Flat area beside river that floods periodically
keyTerms.drainage basin: Area draining into one river system
keyTerms.delta: Fan-shaped deposit where a river meets the sea or lake
keyTerms.tributary: A smaller river flowing into a larger one

quiz.question: Waterfalls form in:
quiz.explanation: Steep gradient, hard/soft rock layers.

quiz.question: Floodplains are fertile because:
quiz.explanation: Fine sediment rich in nutrients.

quiz.question: Drainage basin:
options: Area where all water drains to one river
quiz.explanation: All rainfall flows to the same river.

quiz.question: A delta forms when:
options: A river slows at its mouth and deposits sediment
quiz.explanation: Rivers drop their sediment load when they slow down at the sea.

quiz.question: The water table is:
options: The level below which the ground is saturated with water
quiz.explanation: Below the water table, all spaces in rock and soil are filled with water (groundwater).

lessons.title: Volcanoes and Earthquakes
lessons.content: Volcanoes form where magma reaches Earth's surface — at convergent boundaries (subduction), divergent boundaries (rift zones), and hotspots (like Hawaii). Types: shield (gentle slopes, fluid lava — Mauna Loa), composite/stratovolcano (steep, explosive — Mount Fuji, Vesuvius), and cinder cone (small, steep). Earthquakes occur when stress builds at plate boundaries and releases suddenly. Measured on the Richter scale (logarithmic — each whole number is 10x more powerful). The focus is where the earthquake originates underground; the epicenter is directly above on the surface. Seismic waves spread outward from the focus. Tsunamis are ocean waves triggered by undersea earthquakes. Prediction is difficult, but preparation saves lives: earthquake-resistant buildings, early warning systems, evacuation plans, and public education.
examples: 2010 Haiti earthquake (magnitude 7.0) killed 230,000 — poor construction amplified the disaster
Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE — the preserved city teaches us about Roman life
Japan's earthquake early warning system gives 10-60 seconds warning — enough to take cover

keyTerms.epicenter: The point on Earth's surface directly above where an earthquake originates
keyTerms.tsunami: A large ocean wave caused by an undersea earthquake or volcanic eruption
keyTerms.hotspot: A fixed point of volcanic activity not at a plate boundary (Hawaii, Yellowstone)

quiz.question: The Richter scale is logarithmic, meaning:
options: Each whole number is 10 times more powerful than the one before
quiz.explanation: Magnitude 6 is 10x more powerful than 5, and 100x more than 4.

quiz.question: A hotspot volcano forms:
options: Over a fixed point of heat in the mantle, not at a plate boundary
quiz.explanation: Hawaii formed over a hotspot — the plate moves but the hot spot stays fixed.

quiz.question: Tsunamis are caused by:
options: Undersea earthquakes or volcanic eruptions displacing water
quiz.explanation: The seafloor shifting displaces massive volumes of water, creating huge waves.

quiz.question: Earthquake preparation includes:
options: Building codes, early warning systems, evacuation plans, and public education
Moving away from all fault lines
quiz.explanation: Multiple strategies reduce damage — no single approach is sufficient.

quiz.question: Shield volcanoes have:
options: Gentle slopes and fluid lava — less explosive
Very steep sides and violent eruptions
quiz.explanation: Shield volcanoes (like Mauna Loa) have runny basaltic lava that flows gently — unlike explosive stratovolcanoes.

lessons.title: Coasts and Coastal Processes
lessons.content: Coasts are dynamic environments shaped by waves, tides, wind, and human activity. Erosion processes: hydraulic action (wave force compresses air in rock cracks), abrasion (waves hurl rocks against cliffs), attrition (rocks smash together and get smaller), solution (dissolving soluble rock). Erosion creates landforms: cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches, stacks, and stumps. Deposition occurs where water slows: beaches, spits, bars, and tombolo (sand connecting island to mainland). Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast in the direction of prevailing wind. Coastal management: hard engineering (sea walls, groynes — expensive, can worsen erosion elsewhere) vs soft engineering (beach nourishment, managed retreat — works with nature). Rising sea levels from climate change threaten coastal communities worldwide.
examples: The Twelve Apostles (Australia): limestone stacks formed by erosion of cliff — some have already collapsed
Longshore drift: waves approach at an angle, carry sediment along the coast in a zigzag pattern
Bangladesh: rising sea levels threaten 17 million people living less than 1 meter above sea level

keyTerms.longshore drift: The movement of sediment along a coast by waves approaching at an angle
keyTerms.erosion: The wearing away of coastline by waves, wind, and chemical processes
keyTerms.deposition: The dropping of sediment when water loses energy, forming beaches and spits
keyTerms.hard engineering: Man-made structures to protect coasts (sea walls, groynes) — often expensive and can cause problems elsewhere

quiz.question: Longshore drift moves sediment:
options: Along the coast in the direction of prevailing wind
quiz.explanation: Waves approach at an angle, moving sediment in a zigzag along the shore.

quiz.question: A stack forms when:
options: The roof of a coastal arch collapses, leaving a pillar of rock
quiz.explanation: Erosion sequence: cliff → cave → arch → stack → stump.

quiz.question: Soft engineering coastal management:
options: Works with natural processes — beach nourishment, managed retreat
quiz.explanation: Soft engineering uses nature rather than fighting it — often more sustainable.

quiz.question: Rising sea levels threaten coasts because:
options: More flooding, erosion, and loss of land for coastal communities
quiz.explanation: Millions of people live in low-lying coastal areas vulnerable to even small rises.

quiz.question: Hydraulic action is:
options: Wave force compressing air in rock cracks, breaking the rock apart
quiz.explanation: The sheer force of water and trapped air creates pressure that shatters rock.

lessons.title: Population and Demographics
lessons.content: World population ~8 billion. Demographic transition: Stage 1 (high birth/death, slow growth), Stage 2 (death falls, rapid growth), Stage 3 (birth falls, slowing), Stage 4 (low birth/death, stable). Population pyramids show structure. Overpopulation strains resources; aging populations strain healthcare.
examples: Nigeria: wide pyramid, young growing population
Japan: narrow pyramid, aging
China: one-child policy (1979-2015) created aging population

keyTerms.demographic transition: Shift from high to low birth/death rates
keyTerms.dependency ratio: Ratio of non-working (young + old) to working-age population

quiz.question: Wide-base pyramid:
quiz.explanation: Lots of young people.

quiz.question: Death rates fall first because:
quiz.explanation: Healthcare reduces deaths before birth behavior changes.

quiz.question: World population:
quiz.explanation: Approximately 8 billion.

quiz.question: Dependency ratio matters because:
options: It shows how many people the working-age population must support
quiz.explanation: High dependency = fewer workers supporting more dependents (children + elderly).

quiz.question: Stage 4 of the demographic transition:
options: Low birth and death rates — stable population
quiz.explanation: Most developed countries are in Stage 4 — some face population decline.

lessons.title: Urbanization and Cities
lessons.content: Over 55% of the world lives in cities, expected 68% by 2050. Push factors from rural: poverty, lack of services, disasters. Pull factors to cities: jobs, education, healthcare. Challenges: slums, traffic, pollution, waste, inequality. Smart urban planning: affordable housing, public transport, green spaces.
examples: 1 billion people live in slums globally
Curitiba, Brazil: model city with efficient bus system

keyTerms.push factors: Conditions driving people from rural areas
keyTerms.megacity: A city with more than 10 million people
keyTerms.urban sprawl: Uncontrolled expansion of urban areas into surrounding countryside

quiz.question: World urban population:
quiz.explanation: More than half live in cities.

quiz.question: Push factor:
quiz.explanation: Poverty, lack of services push people out.

quiz.question: Rapid urbanization challenge:
quiz.explanation: Growth outpaces infrastructure.

quiz.question: A megacity has:
quiz.explanation: Lagos, Tokyo, Mumbai, São Paulo — all megacities with 10M+ people.

quiz.question: Urban sprawl causes:
options: Loss of farmland, increased car dependence, and habitat destruction
quiz.explanation: Unplanned expansion creates car-dependent suburbs, eating into green space.

lessons.title: Migration
lessons.content: Internal: within a country. International: between countries. Economic migrants seek better opportunities. Refugees flee war/persecution. Brain drain: educated people leaving developing countries. Remittances: money sent home. Forced migration: slavery, trafficking, conflict/climate displacement.
examples: Filipino workers send ~$30B home annually
Syrian war: 6M+ refugees
Brain drain: African doctors in Europe/America

keyTerms.asylum seeker: A person who has applied for refugee status but hasn't been granted it yet

quiz.question: A refugee:
quiz.explanation: Forced, not chosen.

quiz.question: Remittances:
quiz.explanation: Personal funds transferred to family.

quiz.question: Brain drain:
options: Losing skilled workers to other countries
quiz.explanation: Countries lose critical expertise.

quiz.question: Climate migration is increasing because:
options: Rising seas, drought, and extreme weather make some areas uninhabitable
quiz.explanation: Climate change is becoming a major driver of forced displacement.

quiz.question: The difference between a refugee and an asylum seeker:
options: A refugee has been granted protection; an asylum seeker has applied but is waiting
quiz.explanation: Asylum seekers are in the process — refugees have been officially recognized.

lessons.title: Development and Inequality
lessons.content: Development is more than economic growth — it includes health, education, freedoms, and quality of life. GDP measures economic output but misses inequality, environmental damage, and wellbeing. The Human Development Index (HDI) combines income, life expectancy, and education for a broader picture. Inequality exists between countries (Global North vs South) and within countries (rich vs poor neighborhoods in the same city). Causes of underdevelopment: colonial legacy, unfair trade terms, debt burdens, poor governance, conflict, and disease. Aid comes in many forms: bilateral (country to country), multilateral (through UN/World Bank), NGO projects, and emergency humanitarian relief. Microfinance and fair trade aim to empower communities rather than create dependency. Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising future generations.
examples: Norway HDI = 0.96 (very high), Niger = 0.39 (very low) — shows massive global inequality
Fair trade: farmers get a guaranteed minimum price for coffee, protecting them from market crashes
Microfinance: Grameen Bank in Bangladesh lends small amounts to women entrepreneurs — 97% repayment rate

keyTerms.HDI: Human Development Index — income + life expectancy + education
keyTerms.development: Improvement in living standards, health, education, and opportunities
keyTerms.inequality: Unequal distribution of resources and opportunities
keyTerms.fair trade: Trade ensuring producers in developing countries get fair prices

quiz.question: HDI measures:
options: Income, life expectancy, and education combined
quiz.explanation: HDI gives a broader picture than GDP alone.

quiz.question: GDP doesn't measure:
options: Inequality, environmental damage, or unpaid work
quiz.explanation: A country can have high GDP but massive inequality and environmental destruction.

quiz.question: Fair trade aims to:
options: Ensure producers in developing countries receive fair prices
quiz.explanation: Fair trade gives farmers price stability and better income.

quiz.question: Causes of underdevelopment include:
options: Colonial legacy, unfair trade, debt, poor governance, and conflict
quiz.explanation: Multiple interconnected factors keep some nations from developing.

quiz.question: Sustainable development means:
options: Meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs
quiz.explanation: Balance economic progress with environmental protection and social equity.

lessons.title: Food and Water Security
lessons.content: Food security means all people have access to sufficient, safe, nutritious food at all times. Despite producing enough food globally, 735 million people face hunger — the problem is distribution, not production. Causes of food insecurity: poverty (can't afford food), conflict (disrupts farming and supply), climate change (droughts, floods damage crops), waste (1/3 of all food produced is wasted), and land degradation. Water security is equally critical: 2 billion people lack safe drinking water. Water stress occurs when demand exceeds available supply — regions like the Middle East, North Africa, and parts of India face severe water stress. Solutions include: improving irrigation efficiency, reducing food waste, sustainable farming practices, better storage and distribution in developing countries, and addressing the root causes of poverty. Virtual water: the hidden water used to produce goods — 1 kg of beef requires ~15,000 liters of water.
examples: 1/3 of food produced globally is wasted — enough to feed all hungry people 3 times over
Cape Town 'Day Zero' (2018): the city nearly ran out of water — residents limited to 50 liters/day
Virtual water: a cotton t-shirt requires ~2,700 liters of water to produce

keyTerms.food security: All people having access to sufficient, safe, nutritious food at all times
keyTerms.water stress: When water demand exceeds the available supply in a region
keyTerms.food waste: Edible food that is discarded — 1/3 of global production
keyTerms.virtual water: The total water used in the production of a product

quiz.question: The main cause of hunger is:
options: Poverty and unequal distribution, not insufficient global production
Not enough food is produced globally
quiz.explanation: We produce enough food for 10 billion people — the problem is access and distribution.

quiz.question: 1/3 of all food produced is:
options: Wasted — enough to feed all hungry people several times
quiz.explanation: Food waste is a massive problem — reducing it could dramatically improve food security.

quiz.question: Water stress means:
options: Demand exceeds available supply in a region
quiz.explanation: Growing populations and climate change are increasing water stress worldwide.

quiz.question: Virtual water refers to:
options: The hidden water used to produce goods — a t-shirt needs 2,700 liters
quiz.explanation: Every product has a water footprint — the total water used throughout its production.

quiz.question: Improving food security requires:
options: Reducing waste, sustainable farming, better distribution, and addressing poverty
quiz.explanation: Multiple strategies are needed — production alone isn't enough.

lessons.title: Natural Resources
lessons.content: Renewable resources replenish: solar, wind, water, forests (if managed). Non-renewable are finite: fossil fuels, minerals, metals. Uneven distribution drives trade and geopolitics. Sustainable management: use at a rate that doesn't deplete for future generations.
examples: Saudi Arabia: 17% of global oil reserves
Coltan (for phones) mined in DRC — often exploitatively
Iceland: nearly 100% renewable electricity

keyTerms.fossil fuel: Coal, oil, natural gas from ancient organisms
keyTerms.sustainability: Using resources without depleting them for future generations

quiz.question: Non-renewable:
quiz.explanation: Oil took millions of years to form.

quiz.question: Resource distribution matters because:
options: Uneven distribution drives trade and sometimes conflict
quiz.explanation: Resource-rich countries have economic power.

quiz.question: Sustainable management:
options: Using as much as possible now
quiz.explanation: Balance current needs with future.

quiz.question: Conflict minerals are:
options: Resources whose extraction fuels armed conflict and human rights abuses
quiz.explanation: Coltan, tin, tungsten, and gold from Congo fund armed groups.

quiz.question: The resource curse refers to:
options: Countries rich in resources often having poor governance and slower development
quiz.explanation: Paradoxically, resource wealth can lead to corruption, inequality, and economic distortion.

lessons.title: Climate Change
lessons.content: CO₂ rose from 280 to 420+ ppm since Industrial Revolution. Enhanced greenhouse effect raises temperature ~1.1°C. Effects: melting ice, rising seas, extreme weather, ocean acidification, biodiversity loss. Paris Agreement (2015): limit to 1.5°C.
examples: Arctic ice decreasing ~13% per decade since 1979
Great Barrier Reef coral bleaching from warm oceans
Paris Agreement: 196 countries agreed to reduce emissions

keyTerms.carbon dioxide: Main greenhouse gas from fossil fuels
keyTerms.carbon footprint: Total greenhouse gases produced by a person, event, or product

quiz.question: Enhanced greenhouse effect caused by:
quiz.explanation: More CO₂ traps more heat.

quiz.question: Temperature rise:
quiz.explanation: Enough for significant effects.

quiz.question: Paris Agreement:
quiz.explanation: 196 countries agreed.

quiz.question: Individual carbon footprint can be reduced by:
options: Using public transport, eating less meat, saving energy, and reducing waste
quiz.explanation: Personal choices matter, though systemic change has the biggest impact.

quiz.question: Climate change is a geographic issue because:
options: Its causes and effects are unevenly distributed globally
quiz.explanation: Rich countries cause most emissions; poor countries suffer most consequences.

lessons.title: Conservation and Sustainability
lessons.content: Protected areas cover ~15% of land. CITES protects endangered species. Three pillars: environmental, economic, social. Actions: reduce-reuse-recycle, renewable energy, reforestation, sustainable agriculture. Ecotourism: income while preserving nature. Individual and systemic change both matter.
examples: Kenya wildlife tourism: $1B+ annually
Costa Rica: 20% forest cover (1987) → 50%+ today
Plastic bottle: 450 years to decompose

keyTerms.ecotourism: Tourism conserving environment and benefiting locals
keyTerms.biodiversity hotspot: Area with exceptional species diversity under significant threat

quiz.question: Sustainability pillars:
quiz.explanation: Balance all three.

quiz.question: Ecotourism:
quiz.explanation: Income with minimal environmental impact.

quiz.question: Protected areas cover:
quiz.explanation: Target is 30% by 2030.

quiz.question: Biodiversity hotspots are:
options: Areas with exceptional species diversity under significant threat
quiz.explanation: 25 hotspots contain 44% of all plant species on just 1.4% of land.

quiz.question: The most effective approach to sustainability combines:
options: Individual action AND systemic change (policies, corporate responsibility)
quiz.explanation: Personal choices matter, but structural changes (policy, industry) have the biggest impact.

lessons.title: Energy Geography
lessons.content: Energy consumption varies dramatically worldwide. Developed nations use far more energy per capita than developing nations. Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) still provide ~80% of global energy — but their environmental costs are enormous. Renewable energy is growing fast: solar and wind are now cheaper than new coal in most countries. Nuclear provides carbon-free baseload power but raises safety and waste concerns. Energy poverty: 770 million people lack electricity — mostly in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Access to reliable energy is essential for development: health, education, communication, and economic activity all depend on it. The energy transition from fossil fuels to renewables is the defining challenge of our time — it must happen fast enough to limit climate change while ensuring energy access for all.
examples: An American uses ~300 kWh per capita per month; a Tanzanian uses ~9 kWh — 33x difference
In 2023, renewable energy generated 30% of global electricity — up from 19% in 2000
A single wind turbine can power 1,500 homes — and produces zero emissions during operation

keyTerms.energy poverty: Lack of access to modern energy services — 770 million people lack electricity
keyTerms.energy transition: The global shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources
keyTerms.energy mix: The combination of energy sources a country uses
keyTerms.energy security: Having reliable access to affordable energy

quiz.question: Fossil fuels still provide approximately:
quiz.explanation: Despite growth in renewables, fossil fuels still dominate — making transition urgent.

quiz.question: Energy poverty means:
options: Lacking access to modern energy services like electricity
Energy being expensive in rich countries
quiz.explanation: 770 million people live without electricity — concentrated in Africa and South Asia.

quiz.question: Solar and wind energy are now:
options: Cheaper than new coal in most countries
Always more expensive than fossil fuels
quiz.explanation: Renewable costs have dropped dramatically — solar is now the cheapest electricity source in history.

quiz.question: The energy transition must balance:
options: Speed (climate urgency) with equity (energy access for all)
quiz.explanation: We must cut emissions quickly while ensuring developing nations can access clean energy.

quiz.question: Energy security means:
options: Having reliable access to affordable energy
quiz.explanation: Countries need diverse, reliable, affordable energy — not dependent on any single source or supplier.

lessons.title: Hazard Management
lessons.content: Natural hazards include earthquakes, volcanoes, tropical storms, floods, droughts, and landslides. A hazard becomes a disaster when it affects human populations. Vulnerability depends on: location, poverty (poor communities are most at risk), infrastructure quality, preparedness, and governance. Risk = Hazard × Vulnerability. Reducing risk: prediction and monitoring (seismographs, weather satellites), preparation (building codes, evacuation plans, emergency supplies), protection (flood defenses, earthquake-resistant buildings), and planning (land-use zoning, insurance). Disaster response: immediate rescue and relief, then recovery and rebuilding. Developing countries suffer disproportionately: same earthquake kills thousands in Haiti but few in Japan — the difference is preparation and infrastructure.
examples: Japan: advanced earthquake early warning, strict building codes — saves thousands of lives per earthquake
Haiti 2010: magnitude 7.0 killed 230,000 — similar quake in Japan killed 0 due to building standards
Bangladesh cyclone shelters: raised concrete buildings save lives during annual storms

keyTerms.natural hazard: A natural event with potential to cause harm (earthquake, flood, storm)
keyTerms.vulnerability: How susceptible a population is to a hazard's impact
keyTerms.disaster risk reduction: Actions taken before a hazard to reduce its potential impact
keyTerms.resilience: The ability of a community to withstand and recover from hazards

quiz.question: Risk equals:
options: Hazard × Vulnerability — same hazard is worse where people are more vulnerable
Only the size of the hazard
quiz.explanation: A magnitude 7 earthquake in Tokyo (prepared) vs Haiti (vulnerable) = very different outcomes.

quiz.question: Why do the same hazards kill more people in developing countries?
options: Less preparedness, weaker buildings, less resources for response
quiz.explanation: Poverty, weak infrastructure, and poor governance increase vulnerability.

quiz.question: Disaster risk reduction includes:
options: Prediction, preparation, protection, and planning — BEFORE the hazard hits
Only predicting when it will happen
quiz.explanation: The most effective approach is reducing risk before disasters happen.

quiz.question: Bangladesh reduces cyclone deaths through:
options: Concrete cyclone shelters and early warning systems
quiz.explanation: Cyclone deaths dropped from 500,000 (1970) to under 200 (2020) through shelters and warnings.

quiz.question: Community resilience means:
options: The ability to withstand, adapt to, and recover from hazards
quiz.explanation: Resilient communities prepare, respond effectively, and rebuild stronger after events.

lessons.title: Map Reading
lessons.content: Maps: title, key/legend, scale, compass rose, grid lines. Scale ratio 1:50,000: 1cm = 500m real. Contour lines show height — close = steep, far = gentle. Thematic maps: population density, climate, vegetation. Topographic maps show physical features in detail.
examples: Close contours = cliff
Choropleth: darker = more people

keyTerms.scale: Ratio of map to real distance
keyTerms.contour line: Line connecting points of equal height
keyTerms.topographic map: Map showing physical features with contour lines and symbols

quiz.question: Close contours:
quiz.explanation: Rapid elevation change.

quiz.question: Legend shows:
quiz.explanation: Explains all symbols and colors.

quiz.question: A topographic map shows:
options: Physical features like hills, valleys, rivers using contour lines
quiz.explanation: Topographic maps represent the 3D landscape on a 2D surface.

quiz.question: An isoline map connects:
options: Points of equal value (equal height, temperature, pressure)
quiz.explanation: Contour lines (height), isotherms (temperature), isobars (pressure) are all isolines.

lessons.title: Coordinates and Location
lessons.content: Latitude: N/S of Equator (0-90°). Longitude: E/W of Prime Meridian (0-180°). Written as (lat, lon): Kampala ≈ (0.3°N, 32.6°E). Grid references: eastings (horizontal) then northings (vertical). GPS uses satellites for precise positioning.
examples: London: 51.5°N, 0.1°W
North Pole: 90°N, South Pole: 90°S
GPS: latitude and longitude within meters

keyTerms.longitude: E/W of Prime Meridian in degrees
keyTerms.time zones: Regions with the same standard time, based on longitude (15° = 1 hour)

quiz.question: Latitude measures from:
quiz.explanation: N/S distance from Equator.

quiz.question: Prime Meridian through:
quiz.explanation: 0° longitude.

quiz.question: Kampala (0.3°N, 32.6°E):
quiz.explanation: Close to Equator, east of Prime Meridian.

quiz.question: Time zones are based on:
options: Longitude — 15° of longitude = 1 hour time difference
quiz.explanation: Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours = 15° per hour.

quiz.question: GPS requires signals from:
options: At least 4 satellites for accurate 3D positioning
quiz.explanation: 4 satellites needed: 3 for position, 1 for timing accuracy.

lessons.title: GIS and Modern Geography
lessons.content: GIS captures, stores, analyzes, displays geographic data. Layers different data on maps revealing patterns. GPS gives precise location via satellites. Remote sensing: satellites/drones monitor Earth. Google Earth/Maps brings GIS to everyone. Used for urban planning, disaster management, environmental monitoring.
examples: GIS: layer flood risk + population + hospitals for disaster planning
Satellite tracks Amazon deforestation year by year
Delivery apps use GPS routing for fastest path

lessons.title: Fieldwork and Investigation
lessons.content: Geographical fieldwork involves collecting primary data in the real world to test hypotheses. Steps: formulate a question or hypothesis → choose methods → collect data → process and present → analyze and conclude. Data collection methods: questionnaires (human geography), measurements (river depth, width, speed using a flowmeter), quadrats (sampling squares for vegetation), transects (lines along which you record data), photographs, and sketches. Sampling: random (reduces bias), systematic (at regular intervals), and stratified (proportional to subgroups). Present data: maps, graphs, tables, diagrams. Evaluate: was the sample large enough? Were methods reliable? What could improve next time? Risk assessment is essential — identify hazards before going into the field. Fieldwork skills are transferable: observation, data collection, analysis, and critical thinking.
examples: Hypothesis: 'River velocity increases downstream.' Method: measure speed at 5 points using a flowmeter.
Quadrat sampling: throw a 1m² frame randomly 20 times, count plant species in each — estimate coverage
Risk assessment: working near a river — wear life jackets, work in pairs, check weather forecast

keyTerms.hypothesis: A testable prediction that fieldwork aims to support or reject
keyTerms.quadrat: A sampling frame (usually 1m²) placed randomly to study plant distribution
keyTerms.transect: A line along which data is collected at regular intervals
keyTerms.random sampling: Selecting sample points by chance to reduce bias in results

quiz.question: The first step in fieldwork is:
options: Formulating a question or hypothesis to test
quiz.explanation: Start with a clear question — it guides everything else.

quiz.question: Random sampling reduces:
options: Bias — results are more representative of the whole area
quiz.explanation: Random selection prevents the researcher from choosing only convenient or typical spots.

quiz.question: A quadrat is used to:
options: Sample vegetation by counting species in a defined area
quiz.explanation: Throw the quadrat randomly, count what's inside — repeat many times for reliable data.

quiz.question: Risk assessment before fieldwork:
options: Identifies hazards and plans how to stay safe
quiz.explanation: Even simple fieldwork has risks — weather, traffic, water. Always assess and plan.

quiz.question: Evaluating fieldwork means:
options: Critically assessing whether methods were reliable and results are valid
quiz.explanation: Was the sample big enough? Were conditions fair? What would you change? This reflection is essential.

lessons.title: Geographies of the Future
lessons.content: Geography helps us understand and plan for the future. Urbanization will reshape the world: by 2050, 2/3 of humanity will live in cities — especially in Africa and Asia where urbanization is fastest. Climate change adaptation is a geographical challenge: where to build, where not to build, how to protect vulnerable communities. Technology is transforming geography: drone mapping, real-time satellite monitoring, AI analysis of geographic data, and smart cities using sensors to optimize everything from traffic to energy. Geopolitical shifts: China and India's growing influence, Arctic competition as ice melts, water conflicts in stressed regions. Sustainable development goals provide the framework, but implementation varies dramatically by location. Geographers are essential for navigating these challenges — understanding the spatial dimension of problems is key to solving them.
examples: Smart cities: Barcelona uses sensors in bins that alert collection trucks only when full — 25% cost reduction
AI + geography: machine learning models predict wildfire spread based on terrain, weather, and vegetation data
Water geopolitics: Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam on the Nile creates tension with Egypt and Sudan downstream
